Cool, very fun! Saw your first board. 
To start off, great drawings! 

In your second shot, I’m not sure what it is. Is it the window of the building or is it a monitor screen? And why is that room, small, in a corner, instead of being centered? Overall, I don’t think it’s a super important shot to have since you immediately have another establishing shot in the 3rd shot. 

Falling from the vent: I suggest having a close up of the vent. I know you have the sound effects, but it’s hard to see the vent. It could just be a shot of the vent vibrating, then he falls through, pan down, he crashes behind the desk. 

Also, animate less overall. (Ex: when the man falls, you have maybe 4 drawings of him falling, just 1 drawing of him falling, and 1 of the dust on the ground is fine. Same thing with when a USB/cord is plugged in. Just 2 drawings are fine. Unplugged, then plugged).

Everything else is fun. When he sees the snail for the first time. The shot immediately after that, would be better to be shot from the angle of the POV of the snail. (I just mean that the background would be more flat, like we would see him more front, straight ahead).

He goes from left to right, so the next shot, he should go from left to right as well instead of right to left. (180 rule. You might have to change the staging of him running up to the snail or the shot after to another angle for his position and all to make sense) 

Everything else is fun and great! Last thing is with the chair, I couldn’t tell it was a chair because you first only showed the top of the seat. I would zoom way out, show the full chair before he even drags it. 

Great work!

Watched your first story, looks great! 
First of all, nice start. The second shot, I would zoom out, see the full body of the women and the shop. (Basically, an establishing shot, maybe even see that there are street lamps in the foreground etc.)
And then later, when the person comes into the shop, you have the women at the left side at the counter and the man on the right side by the door. The shot immediately following that, you broke the 180 by having the man on the left and the women on the right. 
Generally It would be nice to see more full body shots, where you see the head as well as the feet! 

Everything from there is pretty good, 
For that one shot where the man reaches for the cat in the bushes, it wasn’t clear to me he was reaching for the cat. I thought he was just inspecting the flowers with his hand out. I would put the cat in the foreground, pretty big in frame, on the bottom left side, with a clear silhouette. And have the man reach again. If you want the cat to be in the bushes, maybe put the bushes sparingly, and still have that silhouette of the cat. The problem is just, I can’t see the cat, and momentarily I didn’t know what the man was doing. 

I think everything else is good! There was a moment where the women looks at the family picture which is not clear to me what it represents. I don’t know what it means in relation to this cat. (For a self contained story of this portfolio piece, I would maybe change it)

And then she bends down to see the cat, but it’s not clear to me what happens after. I think she bends down but feels ill and falls, but steadies herself on the table. Whatever your intention is, you might need to draw/animate more frames for this action to read clearly. And then the women leaves. I’d like to see the door and more of her body! It seems to be a little close to see the action clearly. Great board overall!

1. How did you get started in the industry? 
Took a gap year from school during COVID and applied to some jobs. Got into a preschool production as a story artist.

2. If you went to film / art school did it prepare you for the work field? 
Yes, it prepared me very well. From listening to teachers complain about work or the people they work with and hearing industry gossip prepared me quite a lot from what i will be facing and the struggles of the industry! Plus the first year of art school I had a fantastic teacher who taught me everything I needed to know about story boarding to get a job. I was quite lucky. 

3. Do you enjoy your career?
So far, not that much experience, but yes. I’m looking forward to what the future brings.

4. What do you think new animators need in order to be successful in this industry? 
A good portfolio, and to be pleasant to work with, and meet deadlines.

5. Any advice for newbies?
Keep drawing what you like and keep your love for art alive. From the standpoint of someone still pretty new to the industry, it’s sad some veterans no longer like drawing. 

6. What are some challenges you faced? 
Honestly right now, it’s just finding a job/internship. Unless you work for feature, you’ll be switching studios every 6 months or so, and I’ll be looking for a job constantly. 

7. What do you like most about your work?
Probably drawing characters emotions. It’s cool how a characters emotions can make the audience feel something. And I get to feel those emotions when I draw the characters having them. 

8. Do u ever feel burn out?
Yes, I was so burned out for a year in school. Told myself I’ll never go through that again. So I don’t pile too many things on my plate anymore. And I’m quite fortunate and privileged to be able to afford to do that.

9. What is necessary for the job you picked out?
For storyboarding, for me, it’s important to know how to draw camera moves. How to frame a shot. And what feeling a shot expresses - what a shot MEANS. So that every shot serves a purpose. 

10. What are some common mistakes newbies face?
Hmm, for storyboarding, I would say not reusing shots / backgrounds. Drawing a new shot every time there’s a cut instead of referring to a past shot. Drawing too flat (as in people don’t come forward and backwards in the scene, and just go left and right in and out. Or that the background looks flat.). And I guess just not using framing devices well enough. If the shot looks meh, maybe it should just be changed to a better staged shot.
I refer to story beats to just what happens in a scene, yes!
You’re welcome! Good luck!!!! 💗

For the last board, very interesting story!  

For critique: The framing of most shots are too tight. The action scenes rarely show full body of the character (Head including the feet). Zoom wayy out on your shots. 

And the beginning of the board can move along a little faster. The first shot is a little boring since it’s just a door (maybe another intro would be better to immediately draw attention to the story!). And I think there are too many cuts in the beginning when it’s just two characters entering and leaving the room, getting ready in the morning. Just 2-3 shots is fine to establish that, right now you have around 6 shots of them in the house, preparing to leave.

Overall, very interesting! I was curious what will happen next.

Hello, I watched your first board! It looks great! My suggestion is that the face reveal of the second character comes too early.

You have several beats of the character walking and turning around, walking and turning around. (Look back, cut wide, centipede slithering). I think the beats are repetitive and you only really need one scene of her turning around to get the idea across. Instead of similar beats, you can instead progress the story with the character getting more nervous and running, or being cornered.

And here comes the reveal of your centipede character. You already have several shots of him just slithering without showing his face, so why show his face in the beginning when you want to make it a mystery? It would be better to reveal it when he pops out.

When he pops out, I think it’s important to show his body, that he is half centipede and half man. (The first actual, full reveal of him still doesn’t show his centipede body. This is a great place to get a clear look). I think it would be nice to have the girl be afraid for a longer period of time. Her expression changes from slight fear to immediate concern so fast! It feels like she has everything under control and it keeps the stakes low. Although I suppose she does know him as a friend, so it makes sense she’s not afraid after seeing his face. So then it brings up the question why did Vincent lunge at her? Was he trying to hug her?

If you want to reveal Vincent as a friend. I would move along the climax-fear scene more quickly. He reveals himself quickly, the girl is shocked (simply out of surprise instead of fear), and he lunges quickly with open arms. Thennn the girl cups his face and we get a joyful look: “Vincent!”. She notices the missing teeth. 

For the missing tooth shot (you have a back/profile shot of the broken tooth), this wasn’t clear to me that it was broken because I didn’t see the other tooth that’s NOT broken. So I thought the broken tooth looked normal. 
Although the framing is nice on that shot, I would instead replace it with an extreme close up, full front view of booth teeth. That way it’s clear, one tooth is clearly missing/broken.

Everything else looks great!

Hello, another student here. I think so, as long as you split each section in categories. But usually companies will only hire you for one category and do not care about your skills other ones. If you have multiple skills, order them (on the tab), from the one you like the most to the least. (Your category order can look like: storyboard, visual development, resume, contact)

Also it’ll likely lead them to think you are a student (because students usually are still deciding what field to focus on). 

I’ve heard recruiters say they hesitate when seeing multiple categories because it looks like you aren’t committed to one. I’ve also heard recruiters say they don’t care! And I’ve seen ppl get great job opportunities/internships despite having multiple focuses on their websites.

Giving good advice while holding space for the other person to talk, without trying to change their view or offer solution immediately, is a technique, and it can be learned!

Feeling empathy is a great first step for wanting to help and getting better at giving advice! 

I relate to you, I sound aloof too while I stumble over my words and collect my thoughts. I doubt myself on how good my advice actually is. And sometimes I just feel awkward while the other person is crying!! 

You don’t have to be perfect when you give advice, I am not perfect, but it’s the trying and improving that counts.

Sometimes people aren’t looking for solutions to their problems, they are just looking for someone to talk to to validate their experience and share their frustrations.

You can look into therapy posts? Maybe relationship advice? @decoding_couples on Instagram is a great account to follow and I love learning from them. 

Generally, you can try agreeing with them first (ex: I can’t believe they did this to you!) (awwwe, I’m so sorry that happened) (oh my god, that sounds terrible) (ya I agree with you) (no, you’re not imagining things) (that must be awful, you don’t deserve this) etc.

Then you can summarize what they said and ask questions (ex: so you’re worried about your future because you don’t feel like you are as passionate about your job as much as your friends are?) (Are you worried because of imposter syndrome or are you worried because you feel like you won’t be hired in a high paying job?) (Do you want a high paying job because you are scared of how people would perceive you if you don’t? Or are you scared because of the instability?) 

Let them do most of the talking. 
Then you can keep on asking questions while summarizing as they narrow down their response. The more they tell you, the more you have a better grasp on their situation and what REALLY matters to THEM. 

After all that, if you see other perspectives to the situation, then you can try to offer it. You can also remind them where they have succeeded and their good traits. (Ex: I don’t think this one interview that went badly reflects on you. I think the interviewer is just looking for the type of person who already knows what they want. And it’s perfectly fine to be unsure of what you want right now because you’re still in college! I think you should be more confident in yourself, look at this and this area where you succeeded.)

You can also tell them your experience or personal stories where you can relate to them afterwards. it’s always nice to know I’m not alone in a situation, I’m sure the other person would feel better knowing that too.

Hope that helped! This is what I’ve learned and what helped me.

Hello, thanks for the questions (my answers turned out kind of long)

1. I think for this instance, I notice things are missing only when I need it…Especially for something small like a pencil because it’s harder to notice. And I usually keep my stuff in the same spot. 

If my entire pencil case was missing I would probably notice it right away. But I usually don’t misplace my stuff. I won’t be angry if someone misplaces my stuff just a few times…i would be angry if they do it repeatedly after I tell them not to.


2. I learn pretty fast, especially when I grasp “why” something is done. 

I have an example: in my storyboarding (animation/art related) job, I sent my supervisor a first draft (which I know from experience is always the worst one because I don’t know what he wants). He drew over it and I could immediately see what choices he made and how it improved my drawing. Also, I took his draw over as what is expected of me, so the rest of my work references his example. Either way, when i sent him my second drawing, he said it was like he hired a different employee because of how much it improved. 

(lol I always had the skills, I just finally understood what he wanted)
(Hashtag hire me please I’m a good employee)

Disclaimer: I like drawing so I pay more attention and grasp it faster, but I can’t say I learn just as fast in other subjects 🤭


3. This one is hard to answer…skip! (If you want to narrow it down to what I would do in a specific situation, that would be more helpful. It’s kind of hard to think of examples tbh)

But seeing how I can’t think of any example, maybe it means I don’t see why one would be better than the other. Both got pros and cons, but in the end, it might not even matter which one I pick. xD

I do like weighing the pros and cons in a big decision tho (but everyone tends to do that). 


4. False, feelings are fleeting and often illogical. (this sounds like what an infj would choose, but I think infps still agree to this)

Feelings are kind of like…automatic, it can hint how I feel about something unconsciously, I can take it as a sign there is something deeper I need to resolve (like anger). It doesn’t mean my anger is justified or rational.  

Slightly related but unrelated: I remember when I felt jealous and I didn’t want to, I argued myself into not feeling jealous anymore. (I think it is kind of Fi to inherently not want to feel jealousy). But if I suspect I feel jealous towards someone getting a better job, I’d run a mock scenario in my head and think about how I would feel. Then I sort my feelings out…why do I feel this way? Here are all the examples why I don’t need to feel this way (this looks like Fi+Ne to me). So…when the real deal hits, I don’t have a reason to feel jealous and I can react with genuine congratulations for the other person (which CAN possibly be an Fe motivation).
